title: TrumpFile: a Czechoslovak informant makes an unsupported tax claim about Trump
description_medium: A 1977 Czechoslovak intelligence informant described Donald Trump’s businesses as “completely tax-exempt for the next 30 years,” according to a Guardian report on communist-era files. The quote records what an informant told the StB; it does not verify Trump’s tax status. The file reflected Czechoslovak surveillance of the couple, not a U.S. tax determination.
description_long: The Guardian’s review of Czechoslovak StB files reported that an informant using the cover name Lubos said in 1977 that Donald Trump’s businesses were safe and “completely tax-exempt for the next 30 years.” The informant attributed this to state commissions and an alleged personal relationship with the U.S. president. The article does not establish how the informant reached that conclusion or whether it was accurate. It separately reports that Trump’s wife Ivana was monitored during visits to Czechoslovakia and that the intelligence service collected information about the family. The tax sentence is therefore evidence of what an informant claimed, not a verified tax finding. The title should not present the claim as fact or suggest that Trump was legally exempt from taxes through 2007. The Guardian also notes that later tax records showed Trump could use reported business losses to offset income for a period, a separate issue from the informant’s claim.

corrected_wording.proposed: TrumpFile: a Czechoslovak informant makes an unsupported tax claim about Trump
corrected_wording.reason: The title converts an informant’s unsupported statement in an intelligence file into a factual tax conclusion.

title: Brookings examines Project 2025 proposals for education block grants and school choice
description_medium: Project 2025 proposes converting some federal education funds into block grants, ending Title I funding over time and expanding school-choice policies. Brookings describes these as proposals and discusses trade-offs, including reduced federal accountability. Those proposals could affect school resources, but the supplied sources do not show completed nationwide resegregation.
description_long: Project 2025’s education chapter proposes changing how the federal government distributes education money. Brookings explains that the plan would initially make Title I a “no-strings-attached” block grant and phase out federal Title I spending over ten years, leaving states to decide whether to replace it. The analysis notes that some federal education programs are already block grants and explains that shifting funds to states would reduce federal restrictions and oversight. Separately, school-choice and voucher policies can change which schools receive public support and how families access them. Civil-rights advocates warn that these changes could deepen inequality or weaken protections for disadvantaged students, but predicted effects should be distinguished from measured enrollment or resource changes. The supplied articles describe policy proposals and risks; they do not establish that Trump implemented nationwide school resegregation or abolished Title I protections. The entry should center on the proposed funding shift and clearly label its potential consequences as forecasts.

title: FBI agents discuss Atlantic City casino plans and an undercover operation with Trump
description_medium: In April 1981, FBI agents met Donald Trump in his Manhattan office after his labor consultant Daniel Sullivan introduced them. Trump discussed his Atlantic City casino plans and suggested undercover agents work inside a future casino. The Washington Post reports that the proposal was developed but apparently never carried out; the record does not show Trump asked for personal protection.
description_long: The Washington Post’s account, based on FBI reports, legal records and interviews, describes an April 1981 meeting between Donald Trump, labor consultant Daniel Sullivan and FBI agents Walt Stowe and Damon Taylor. Sullivan was an FBI informant, and the agents wanted to discuss organized crime as Trump prepared to enter the Atlantic City casino business. Trump told them about his plans and offered to cooperate if the casino proceeded. An FBI report records his suggestion that undercover agents work inside the casino. The agents developed the idea, but the proposal apparently never came to fruition. Later, New Jersey gaming regulators scrutinized Trump’s relationship with Sullivan, and Trump said he would end dealings with him except as a lessor. The reporting documents meetings and a proposed operation, not a request by Trump for personal protection or proof that the operation was approved.

corrected_wording.reason: The source records FBI meetings and an unimplemented undercover proposal, not a request for personal protection.

title: TWA asks federal regulators to block Carl Icahn’s 1985 takeover bid
description_medium: In May 1985, Trans World Airlines asked the Department of Transportation to block Carl Icahn’s hostile takeover bid, arguing that he lacked airline-management experience and a sound operating plan. Icahn held about 23 percent of TWA. The filing began a public regulatory fight; it did not itself determine TWA’s later ownership or the effects on St. Louis.
description_long: On May 16, 1985, Trans World Airlines asked the Department of Transportation to prevent financier Carl Icahn from taking control of the airline. TWA argued that Icahn was buying stock for a quick profit, lacked experience operating an airline and was not fit to control a major carrier. At the time, Icahn’s investor group held about 23 percent of TWA. The airline asked the department to investigate whether it would remain fit to operate if Icahn gained control and to modify its operating certificates to block the takeover. The filing was an unusual attempt to use aviation regulation in a corporate takeover contest. Later that month TWA’s directors voted to sell the company after a federal judge declined to block Icahn’s bid; TWA ultimately agreed to be acquired by Texas Air, and Icahn later gained control. Those later developments, rather than the May filing alone, shaped the company’s ownership and its St. Louis hub.

corrected_wording.reason: The original title asserts broad regional damage and an outcome not established by the cited May filing.

title: A former Israeli intelligence employee alleges Maxwell tipped off Mossad about Vanunu
description_medium: Ari Ben-Menashe, who described himself as a former Israeli intelligence employee, alleged that Robert Maxwell told Israel about nuclear technician Mordechai Vanunu’s disclosures in 1986. The claim is disputed and the linked timeline does not provide documentary proof. Vanunu’s disclosure and later abduction are documented separately from the allegation about Maxwell.
description_long: Mordechai Vanunu, a former technician at Israel’s Dimona nuclear facility, gave photographs and information about the country’s nuclear program to the Sunday Times in 1986. He disappeared in Rome that autumn and was brought to Israel, where he was tried and imprisoned. A separate allegation that publisher Robert Maxwell tipped off Israeli intelligence came from Ari Ben-Menashe, who presented himself as a former Israeli intelligence employee. Amnesty International notes that this allegation arose after Vanunu’s disclosure and should not be treated as established fact. TrumpFile’s timeline repeats the claim but does not supply a documentary record showing what Maxwell told Israeli officials or when. A careful account can describe Vanunu’s documented disclosure and the subsequent allegation, while making clear that Maxwell’s role remains unverified. The available evidence does not support presenting the alleged tip as a confirmed event.

description_long: Donald Trump visited Moscow and Leningrad in the summer of 1987 after an invitation from a Soviet state agency, according to reporting by the Guardian.
